title: Yukon gov't to review school worksheet about 'positive aspects' of residential schools
summary: The Yukon Department of Education says it will review its Grade 10 curriculum after concerns were raised about a worksheet given to students asking about "positive aspects" of residential schools.

image.caption: The Yukon Department of Education building in Whitehorse. The education minister said the contentious worksheet is just one piece of a broader Grade 10 curriculum that was developed in consultation with First Nations elders and survivors. (CBC)

blocks.text: North·New
The Yukon Department of Education says it will review its Grade 10 curriculum after concerns were raised about a worksheet given to students asking about "positive aspects" of residential schools.
'Maybe it’s [a question] better discussed in a group setting,' education minister says

A photo of the worksheet was recently posted on social media by someone who said it showed a page from their child's homework. The Yukon government confirmed to CBC News that the image matches a real worksheet used as part of the curriculum.
One question on the sheet referred to a residential school survivor "who had attended the Carcross Indian Residential School."

"He and some other former residential school students from Yukon insist that although there were unquestionably a lot of negative experiences at these schools, there were also many positives. What do you think were some of the positive aspects of residential school?” the question reads.

Francis van Kessel, a Teslin Tlingit woman who has family members who went to residential school, says she was disturbed and angry when she saw the classroom material. She sent a seven-page letter this month to the minister of education, calling for the immediate removal of the material and for a comprehensive review of how residential school history is taught in Yukon schools.
"There is an enormous difference between acknowledging a survivor's positive personal memories and asking students to identify aspects of the residential school system itself," states her letter.

In a statement to CBC News, the Yukon First Nations Education Directorate also weighed in, acknowledging that "there exist a few positive experiences recounted by a very small number of elders" who went to residential school. However, the statement says overall, the system was a "wholly negative attempt at cultural genocide."
"By no means should these rare experiences provide justification for an argument that there were 'some positive aspects of residential schools,'" the statement reads.

In an interview with CBC News, Scott Kent, Yukon's minister of education, said the worksheet is just one piece of a broader Grade 10 curriculum that was developed in consultation with First Nations, "including elders and survivors."
“What caused a lot of concern was that it was sent home as a worksheet, for students to work on at home,” said Kent. “Maybe it’s [a question] better discussed in a group setting.”

'It’s probably time to take a look at it and make sure it’s meeting the needs of students,' said Education Minister Scott Kent, seen here earlier this year, about the curriculum material. (Dana Hatherly/CBC)

In a statement to CBC News, the Department of Education says a review will be done to consider whether sensitive materials should be delivered though guided classroom discussions, rather than through activities completed by students on their own.
Dialogue, not worksheets

Joanne Henry is a residential school survivor and the executive director of the Committee on Abuse in Residential Schools (CAIRS) Yukon. She was also part of the group that had developed the curriculum years ago.
She said the original plan was for the residential school material to be delivered in the classroom.
“Part of it was to invite an elder in and also a residential school survivor for them to tell their story,” said Henry.
Henry has shared her personal history in classrooms before, and said it is important not to discredit anyone's experience.
“When I tell my story, I do tell about the good things that happened in there,” she added, citing the fact that she made some lifelong friends at the school.
But, she said, “the negative far, far, far overshadows anything positive about residential school.”
The memory of meeting a friend is paired with the feeling of realizing as she walked through the school doors that her mom was gone, she explained.
Henry said she's heard of people who attended residential school and do have positive memories, even if that wasn’t her experience.
“There’s nothing wrong with that," she said — adding that that kind of nuance can be better covered in a dialogue.
Where did the worksheet come from?
The contentious worksheet is one activity included in "Our Stories of Residential Schools in Yukon and Canada," a teacher resource for the Grade 10 residential school curriculum.
It was made available to Yukon schools in October 2024, as part of annual training provided to new social studies teachers, according to the Department of Education.
The department says it does not centrally track which schools, teachers, or students have used this specific material.
“It’s probably time to take a look at it and make sure it’s meeting the needs of students as well as the delivery of the course,” Kent said.

The details of the department's planned review and when it will be conducted have not yet been determined, explained Kent. However, he says the review will ideally include members of the original curriculum working group.
"But, there are others that we can rely on, other survivors or elders or knowledge keepers," he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Grace Knapp is an associate producer at CBC Whitehorse. She was previously the Mary McGuire Scholar with CBC North.
